packs.title: Park to Coast
packs.promise: Find industrial traces, park geometry and coastal views beyond the central harbour.

q.s: Turn a rolling park view into a small original landscape.
st: From a stopped public path, find the curved line of a grassy hill and the more angular line of buildings or brick stacks behind it. You can use the council’s hill photograph.
Invent a small landscape on your own paper or device using one curve and one angular line. Change their proportions to make your own composition.
Save your two-line landscape and explain which line you chose to make stronger. This is an illustration, not a measured elevation profile or map.

q.s: Collect the geometry of a pavilion without entering it.
st: Find a broad circular band, a domed roof and an opening between supporting columns, or use the architect’s photograph.
Record the three forms as simple shapes: a curve, a dome outline and an open gap. Compare how the solid band and open gap change the building’s apparent weight.
Keep the shapes together with one sentence about the comparison. You do not need to read, copy or rub any lettering on the pavilion.

q.s: Make an original small palette at a beachside park.
st: Find three colours belonging to the setting: a sandstone band, the park’s planting and the sea or sky. Describe the colours without collecting anything.
Invent three small colour marks on your own paper or device. Arrange them into an original palette that reflects the relationship you noticed. A word palette works equally well.
Save the marks or colour words with a short title of your own. Exclude people, shop lettering, flags and existing artworks from your palette.

packs.title: Harbour in the Details
packs.promise: Find your own small story around a very big harbour.

q.s: Read a small part of The Rocks through its materials.
st: Begin at the George Street and Argyle Street corner. Choose a short stretch of public footpath with room to pause.
Find three material contrasts: coarse stone beside a smooth surface, a dark metal detail beside a light wall, and a straight edge against open sky. Looking is enough; do not touch a building.
For each contrast, write two descriptive words. Keep the six words as a tiny material glossary.
Choose the pair that best captures this particular street. Save it with the other observations.

q.s: Make a postcard that could only belong to this moment.
st: Choose an open part of the Campbells Cove promenade, away from restaurant doors and port barriers.
Pick one near detail and one distant detail: perhaps a stone edge close by and a ferry, arch or patch of water farther away.
Write a postcard caption of exactly six words that connects those two details. It can be playful, quiet or surprising.
Save the six words with a photo of the view or describe the two details in a note.

q.s: Collect differences while leaving every plant in place.
st: Enter through an open public Garden gate during posted hours. Choose three leaves you can see from a permitted path without reaching into a planted bed.
Compare their outlines, edges and how the light passes across them. A broad leaf, a narrow leaf or a cluster can each supply a different word.
Invent one descriptive word for each leaf, using shape or light rather than guessing its species or cultural use.
Save the three words and their observed features as a note or photographs of leaves still on their plants.
